# https://clawbackshield.netlify.app/social-security-overpayment-waiver

Overpayment waiver

## Social Security overpayment waiver: how to ask SSA to forgive it
A waiver asks SSA to drop the debt even if their math is right. You qualify if the overpayment wasn't your fault and paying it back would be a hardship or unfair. It's free to ask, and you can ask at any time.
Updated October 2026 · Not legal advice · Not affiliated with SSA
Got a notice right now? Paste it in free and we'll show the amount, the deadlines and your options in plain English.

## Quick answers

- Who qualifies for a Social Security overpayment waiver?
SSA must waive recovery when you were not at fault and repaying would either defeat the purpose of benefits (you need the money for ordinary living expenses) or be against equity and good conscience. Source: 20 CFR 404.506, 20 CFR 416.550

- Is there a deadline to ask for a waiver?
No. You can ask for a waiver at any time. Asking within 30 days of the notice generally keeps SSA from starting to withhold until it decides. Source: SSA: Resolve an overpayment

- What is the difference between a waiver and an appeal?
A waiver (Form SSA-632-BK) asks SSA not to collect even if the amount is right. An appeal, called reconsideration (Form SSA-561), says the amount or facts are wrong and has a 60-day deadline. You can file both. Source: Form SSA-632-BK, Form SSA-561

- Should I appeal or ask for a waiver?
Appeal (reconsideration, SSA-561) if you think you were not overpaid or the amount is wrong. Ask for a waiver if the amount is right but it was not your fault and repaying is a hardship or unfair. Use our 1-minute chooser at /appeal-or-waiver. Source: SSA: Resolve an overpayment, SSA POMS GN 02201.025

## Who qualifies

Under the law (20 CFR 404.506 for Social Security, 20 CFR 416.550 for SSI), SSA must waive recovery when both are true:
- You were not at fault. You reported changes, gave correct information, or reasonably didn't know the rules. SSA's own delays count in your favor.
- Repaying would defeat the purpose of benefits (you need the money for ordinary living expenses), or it would be unfair ("against equity and good conscience"), for example you gave up something relying on the payments.
If you or your parent were "at fault," a waiver is unlikely. An appeal or a lower payment plan may fit better.

## Waiver vs. appeal

A waiver (Form SSA-632-BK) says: "Maybe we were overpaid, but don't make us pay it back." An appeal, called reconsideration (Form SSA-561), says: "Your amount or facts are wrong." You can file both. Appeals have a 60-day deadline. Waivers don't.
Not sure which? Take the 1-minute chooser, or read the SSA-561 reconsideration guide.

## How to ask, step by step

- Check the amount. If the original overpayment is $2,000 or less, call first. SSA can often waive it by phone. See waiver by phone.
- Fill out Form SSA-632-BK. Explain why it wasn't your fault and list income, expenses and assets.
- Attach proof: the notice, bank statements, bills, and any record that you reported changes.
- Send it to your local SSA office by mail (keep proof), fax, or in person. Keep a full copy.
- Ask SSA to pause withholding while it decides. See how to stop withholding.
- Call about two weeks later to confirm it's on file. Write down the date and name.

## Deadlines that matter

You can ask for a waiver any time, even after money is being taken. But asking within 30 days of getting the notice generally keeps SSA from starting to withhold until it decides. SSI notices may give 10 days, so check yours.

## If SSA says no

Before denying a waiver, SSA generally must offer a personal conference, a chance to explain in person or by phone. Go, and bring your proof. If it's still denied, you can ask for reconsideration within 60 days, then a hearing. Free legal aid can help: lawhelp.org.

## Helping a parent?

You can do the work. Your parent (or you, as representative payee or with power of attorney) signs. ClawbackShield has an "I'm helping a parent" mode that words everything for you. Start a case.

## Want it done right, step by step?
Build the waiver or appeal, get a pause-withholding letter, and track it until SSA decides. $299 per case. Notice explanation is free.

# https://clawbackshield.netlify.app/ssa-632-guide

SSA-632 guide

## SSA-632 and SSA-632-BK: how to fill out the waiver form
SSA-632-BK is the official Request for Waiver of Overpayment Recovery. People call it the SSA-632. It's the same form. Here's what it asks and how to answer it well.
Updated October 2026 · Not legal advice · Not affiliated with SSA
Got a notice right now? Paste it in free and we'll show the amount, the deadlines and your options in plain English.

## Quick answers

- Is SSA-632 the same as SSA-632-BK?
Yes. SSA-632-BK is the current form number for the Request for Waiver of Overpayment Recovery; people often call it the SSA-632. The form is free from ssa.gov. Source: Form SSA-632-BK

- Which form do I use if I think the amount is wrong?
Use Form SSA-561 to request reconsideration. To ask only for a smaller monthly repayment, use Form SSA-634. Source: Form SSA-561, Form SSA-634

- Do I need the form for a small overpayment?
For an original overpayment of $2,000 or less, SSA can often take the waiver request by phone at 1-800-772-1213. Source: SSA POMS GN 02250.350

## SSA-632 vs. SSA-632-BK

"SSA-632-BK" is the current form number (the BK marks the booklet version). "SSA-632" is shorthand. Use the latest version from ssa.gov/forms/ssa-632-bk.pdf. It's free. Never pay for the form itself.

## When to use it, and when not to

Use it if the overpayment wasn't your fault and you can't afford to repay, or repaying would be unfair.
- Think the amount is wrong? That's an appeal: see the SSA-561 guide or the appeal-or-waiver chooser.
- $2,000 or less? The form itself tells you to call 1-800-772-1213 instead. See waiver by phone.
- Think the amount is wrong? Use SSA-561 (reconsideration).
- Only want smaller monthly payments? Use SSA-634.

## What the form asks

- About the overpayment: amount, the notice, and whose benefits.
- Why you want a waiver: not your fault, can't afford it, or unfair for other reasons. Check all that apply.
- Fault questions: what you knew, what you reported, when, and how. Be specific: dates, names, phone or office visits.
- Household and finances: who lives with you, monthly income, monthly expenses, and assets (cash, bank accounts, investments, extra property).
- Signature: the beneficiary, or the representative payee / legal guardian.

## Tips that make a difference

- Tell the story in order: what changed, when you told SSA, what SSA did (or didn't do).
- Use real monthly numbers. If expenses meet or exceed income, say so plainly.
- Attach proof: bank statements (about 3 months), bills, medical costs, and any record of reporting.
- Fill every section that applies. Blank answers slow things down.
- Keep a full copy and proof of mailing or a fax confirmation.

## Where to send it

Mail or fax it to your local Social Security office (find it at ssa.gov office locator), or hand it in. If money is being taken, also send a request to pause withholding. See stop withholding.

## Let us pre-fill the answers

ClawbackShield turns your situation into SSA-632 answers you can copy onto the form, plus a fault argument, hardship statement and cover letter. Start a case ($299 per case; reading your notice is free).

# https://clawbackshield.netlify.app/stop-overpayment-withholding

Stop withholding

## How to stop SSA from withholding the check
For Social Security overpayment notices sent since April 25, 2025, SSA's default is to withhold 50% of the monthly check (SSI stays at 10%). You have real ways to pause or shrink that.
Updated October 2026 · Not legal advice · Not affiliated with SSA
Got a notice right now? Paste it in free and we'll show the amount, the deadlines and your options in plain English.

## Quick answers

- How much can SSA withhold for an overpayment?
For Social Security overpayment notices sent on or after April 25, 2025, SSA's default withholding is 50% of the monthly benefit. For SSI, the default is 10% of monthly income. Source: SSA: Resolve an overpayment

- How do I stop SSA from withholding my check?
File a waiver (SSA-632-BK) or an appeal (SSA-561) within 30 days of getting the notice; SSA generally will not start withholding until it decides. If you file later, ask SSA in writing to stop recovery while it reviews. Source: Form SSA-632-BK, Form SSA-561, SSA: Resolve an overpayment

- Can I lower the monthly withholding?
Yes. Use Form SSA-634, Request for Change in Overpayment Recovery Rate, or ask by phone at 1-800-772-1213. Source: Form SSA-634

## The current rules

- Social Security (retirement, survivors, SSDI): default withholding is 50% of the monthly benefit for notices sent on or after April 25, 2025 (SSA EM-25029).
- SSI: default is 10% of monthly income.
- Withholding usually starts after your appeal window, so you have time if you act fast.

## 1. Ask for a waiver or appeal within 30 days

If you file a waiver (SSA-632-BK) or an appeal (SSA-561) within 30 days of getting the notice, SSA generally won't start withholding until it decides. SSI notices may say 10 days. Check yours. Asking later still counts. Just ask SSA to stop recovery while it reviews.

## 2. Send a pause request in writing

Put it in writing: "A waiver request was filed on [date]. Please stop recovery until it is decided and refund anything withheld since." Keep proof you sent it. ClawbackShield generates this letter from your case details.

## 3. Ask for a lower monthly amount (SSA-634)

If you'll repay some or all of it, use Form SSA-634 (Request for Change in Overpayment Recovery Rate) to ask for a smaller withholding based on your income and expenses. You can also ask by phone at 1-800-772-1213.

## 4. Small overpayment? Ask for a phone waiver

If the original overpayment is $2,000 or less and you weren't at fault, SSA can often waive it over the phone. See waiver by phone.

## If money was already taken

If SSA approves your waiver, ask it to refund what was withheld after you asked. Keep the decision letter and your records of what was taken.

## Get organized fast

Read your notice free to see your exact deadlines, then learn how waivers work.

# https://clawbackshield.netlify.app/waiver-by-phone

Waiver by phone

## Overpayment of $2,000 or less? Try a free phone call first.
SSA can often waive small overpayments over the phone, with no SSA-632 form, if it can presume you weren't at fault. It's free. You may not need us or anyone else.
Updated October 2026 · Not legal advice · Not affiliated with SSA
Got a notice right now? Paste it in free and we'll show the amount, the deadlines and your options in plain English.

## Quick answers

- Can SSA waive an overpayment by phone?
Often, yes. If the original overpayment is $2,000 or less and SSA can presume you were not at fault, SSA can usually take the waiver request by phone with no SSA-632 form. The limit has changed over time, so ask. Source: SSA POMS GN 02250.350

- What number do I call?
Call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), or call or visit your local Social Security office. Source: SSA: Resolve an overpayment

- What if the amount is over $2,000?
Use Form SSA-632-BK, the Request for Waiver of Overpayment Recovery. SSA can help you complete it. Source: Form SSA-632-BK, SSA POMS GN 02250.350

## Who this works for

- The original overpayment amount (not what's left) is $2,000 or less.
- SSA can presume you weren't at fault (for example, you didn't hide anything and SSA didn't find fraud).
- Works for both Social Security and SSI (SSA POMS GN 02250.350).
The limit used to be $1,000 and has changed over time, so always ask.

## How to ask

- Call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), or call or visit your local office.
- Say: "I'd like to request a waiver of my overpayment. The original amount is under $2,000 and it wasn't my fault."
- Have the notice ready, and ideally the beneficiary on the line (or your representative payee / power of attorney details).
- Write down the date, time, the person's name, and what they said.
- Ask them to confirm the waiver in writing and to stop any withholding.

## If they say you need the form

If SSA can't presume you weren't at fault, or the amount is over $2,000, you'll need the full waiver: Form SSA-632-BK. SSA can also help you complete it over the phone. If you think the amount itself is wrong, that's an SSA-561 appeal.

## Honest note from us

For small, clear-cut cases, the phone call is usually the fastest and cheapest path. It's free. ClawbackShield is most useful for larger amounts, messy fault questions, or when you're handling it for a parent and need everything organized. Reading your notice with us is always free.

# https://clawbackshield.netlify.app/ssa-561-reconsideration

SSA-561 reconsideration

## SSA-561: how to appeal an overpayment you think is wrong
If SSA's numbers or facts are wrong, don't ask for forgiveness. Ask for a recount. Form SSA-561 makes SSA look again. You have 60 days, and filing within 30 keeps your check whole while they decide.
Updated October 2026 · Not legal advice · Not affiliated with SSA
Got a notice right now? Paste it in free and we'll show the amount, the deadlines and your options in plain English.

## Quick answers

- What is SSA-561 reconsideration for an overpayment?
It is the first level of appeal. You ask SSA to look again because you think you were not overpaid, or the amount is wrong. Source: 20 CFR 404.502a, SSA POMS GN 02201.025

- What is the deadline to file SSA-561?
SSA must get your written request within 60 days after you receive the notice. SSA assumes you received it 5 days after the date on the notice. If you miss it, you can ask in writing for more time and explain your good cause. Source: 20 CFR 404.909, 20 CFR 416.1409, 20 CFR 404.901

- Should I file SSA-561 or SSA-632?
File SSA-561 if you disagree with the overpayment or its amount. File SSA-632 (waiver) if the amount is right but it was not your fault and you can't afford to repay or repaying is unfair. You can file both. Source: SSA: Resolve an overpayment, SSA POMS GN 02201.025

- Will SSA stop withholding while I appeal?
If you ask for an appeal or waiver within 30 days, SSA says it won't collect until it decides on your request. Source: SSA: Resolve an overpayment, 20 CFR 404.502a

## What reconsideration is

Every overpayment notice must explain your right to ask SSA to reconsider the fact or the amount of the overpayment (20 CFR 404.502a). It's the first step of appeal.
Use it when you think:
- You weren't overpaid at all, for example "I didn't work in those months."
- The amount is wrong, for example SSA counted income you never got.
SSA's own staff are told the reason should be specific, like "I did not work" or "I did not receive a pension," not just "I disagree" (POMS GN 02201.025).

## Reconsideration or waiver?

- Amount or facts wrong? Reconsideration, Form SSA-561.
- Amount right, but not your fault and you can't afford it (or it's unfair)? Waiver, Form SSA-632-BK.
- Both? File both. SSA's rules expect people to send an SSA-632-BK together with a reconsideration request.
SSA says an appeal should only be filed if you disagree with the overpayment amount. Not sure? Take the 1-minute chooser.

## The 60-day deadline

- SSA must get your written request within 60 days after you receive the notice (20 CFR 404.909 for Social Security, 416.1409 for SSI).
- SSA assumes you received it 5 days after the date on the notice, unless you show it came later (20 CFR 404.901). So count 65 days from the printed date.
- Missed it? Ask for more time in writing and explain why. SSA extends the deadline if you show good cause.
- A waiver has no deadline. An appeal does. If you're close to day 60, file the appeal first.

## How to request it

- Get Form SSA-561, or file a non-medical appeal online from the same SSA page.
- In the reason box, say exactly what's wrong, in one or two sentences.
- Attach proof: pay stubs, bank statements, SSA letters, records that you reported changes.
- Send it to your local Social Security office. Keep a full copy and proof of when you sent it.
- Need help? Call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). SSA offices will help you complete appeal forms.

## Ask SSA to pause withholding

SSA says: if you ask for a waiver or appeal within 30 days, it won't collect the money until it decides on your request. After that, it automatically withholds 50% of a Social Security benefit or 10% of an SSI payment.
So: file early, and say in your cover letter that you want collection stopped while the appeal is reviewed. Already being withheld? Still ask. See how to stop withholding. If a lower monthly amount is what you need, that's Form SSA-634.

## Small overpayment? $2,000 or less

For Social Security (Title II) overpayments of $2,000 or less, SSA's rules say to treat your appeal as a waiver request too, and to look at that waiver if the appeal doesn't fully win (POMS GN 02201.025). You may also be able to ask for the waiver by phone.

## If SSA says no

SSA sends a reconsideration decision that explains your right to ask for a hearing and to ask for a waiver. For Social Security overpayments, that notice says collection can begin or resume in 60 days even if you ask for a hearing, but a waiver request stops it until SSA decides (POMS GN 02201.025). Free legal aid can help: lawhelp.org.

## How it fits your ClawbackShield case

Pick Appeal (SSA-561) or Both when you start a case. Your case timeline then shows:
- The 30-day date to keep withholding from starting.
- The 60-day appeal date, counted from 5 days after the notice date.
- After you file: call-SSA and follow-up reminders, and a letter asking SSA to pause withholding.
- If SSA denies, a new 60-day reminder to appeal the denial.
Start an appeal case or read your notice free first.

## Not legal advice

This is general information from SSA's published rules, not legal advice. Your notice's dates control. Confirm at ssa.gov or with a lawyer or legal aid.

# https://clawbackshield.netlify.app/appeal-or-waiver

Appeal or waiver?

## Appeal or waiver? Find your path in one minute.

## Quick answers

- How do I appeal an SSA overpayment?
File Form SSA-561, Request for Reconsideration, or a non-medical appeal online. SSA must get it in writing within 60 days after you receive the notice, which SSA assumes is 5 days after its date. Source: Form SSA-561, 20 CFR 404.909, 20 CFR 404.901

- When should I appeal instead of asking for a waiver?
Appeal if you think you weren't overpaid or the amount is wrong. Ask for a waiver if the amount is right but it wasn't your fault and you can't afford to repay or repaying is unfair. Source: SSA: Resolve an overpayment

- Can I appeal and ask for a waiver at the same time?
Yes. SSA's procedures cover a signed SSA-632-BK sent with a reconsideration request. Source: SSA POMS GN 02201.025

- Is there a faster option for small overpayments?
If the original overpayment is $2,000 or less and SSA can presume you weren't at fault, it can often take the waiver by phone. Source: SSA POMS GN 02250.350

## The short version

- Appeal (SSA-561): "You got it wrong." 60-day deadline (20 CFR 404.909, 416.1409).
- Waiver (SSA-632-BK): "Right amount, but not my fault and I can't pay." No deadline (20 CFR 404.506, 416.550).
- Either one within 30 days: SSA says it won't collect until it decides.

## Not legal advice

This tool gives general information based on SSA's published rules. It isn't legal advice and doesn't decide your case. Your notice's dates control. When in doubt, call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 or free legal aid at lawhelp.org.
